title: The sound behind Sinatra: harmon mute and the Playboy poll
summary: Sinatra requested Edison, who had his own stand and played freely with a harmon mute; it made his popularity and won a poll.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: Yeah, I have so much fun playing with Frank Sinatra. And that was in '52 and I played with him six years, right here. Made all the recordings with him and a lot of times I would go on the date. They would have like four trumpets and have like another stand over there, you know, just for me. And I'd put earphones on and just listen to him sing and play what I wanted to play, you know. Wouldn't have to play the music.
Well, you know, that goes back to what we were saying about the individuality of sound. I mean, that's what that is, isn't it.
I mean, certainly plenty of trumpet players could play all the notes that you play but they don't play them that way.
It was really a very big compliment.
Oh, yeah, and it was a compliment to me for him to request me all the time. And the sound behind him became -- people looked for that sound, you know. It became --
Did you mostly play with the harmon mute?
Oh, yeah, all the time. And then, that was -- after about '56, I went back to New York. Well, that was the beginning of my popularity, playing behind him.
Yes, I suppose so. It made a much bigger thing of it.
Yes. Then I won the "Playboy" thing one year, you know, playing behind Best Accompanying trumpet players, you know. And then after about '56 -- '57 I went back to New York and formed my own band.
